Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”), 1 the current transmission providers enrolled

in the WestConnect planning region for purposes of Long-Term Regional Transmission Planning2

 (“Transmission Providers”)3 hereby provide this motion for leave to answer and answer

(“Answer”) regarding the motion for leave to answer and answer filed by the CREPC 1920 Ad

Commission accept this Answer and accept the Transmission Providers’ compliance filings

submitted in response to Order No. 1920 (the “June 12th Compliance Filings”).

        As demonstrated by the June 12th Compliance Filings, and despite the Ad Hoc

Committee’s Answer claims to the contrary, the Transmission Providers’ proposed tariff changes

fully address each directive in Order No. 1920 to implement Long-Term Regional Transmission

Planning within the WestConnect planning region and should be accepted as filed. 5

 I.      Background

        On June 12, 2026, the Transmission Providers submitted substantially identical compliance

filings in their respective dockets to implement the long-term regional transmission planning

requirements of Order Nos. 1920, 1920-A, and 1920-B (“Order No. 1920”). 6

        Following the submission of comments and protests, the Transmission Providers filed an

Answer on August 20, 2026. This Answer resulted in an additional round of comments and

protests, which the Transmission Providers responded to on September 23, 2026. In response, the

Ad Hoc Committee filed an Answer on October 2, 2026.

        The Ad Hoc Committee’s October 2 Answer asks the Commission to accept its proposed

ex ante cost allocation methodology7 and State Agreement Process proposals8 despite the flaws

that make the proposal unlawful in certain respects and unworkable in the WestConnect region in

other respects. The Ad Hoc Committee’s October 2 Answer also responds to several of the

Transmission Providers’ criticisms of the methodology and proposal. The Ad Hoc Committee

asserts that FERC has the latitude to approve their proposed ex ante cost allocation methodology

under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”). 9 It argues that the process used to reach this

methodology was in keeping with Order No. 1920’s requirements and asserts that there is enough

detail for the Commission to approve it. The Ad Hoc Committee also asserts that key provisions

of the methodology, such as the subscription process, 10 the use of DFAX to determine regional

Order No. 1920.

        The Ad Hoc Committee also urges the Commission to accept their proposed State

Agreement Process.13 It contends that the State Agreement Process was selected by state regulators

in keeping with the flexibility provided by Order No. 1920. 14 The Ad Hoc Committee objects to

the Transmission Providers’ decision not to file its proposal (although, as required by Order No.

1920-A, the proposal was, in fact, filed),15 and asserts that information-sharing provisions within

it are necessary to enable effective regulation. 16 Furthermore, although unrelated to the State

Agreement Process, the Ad Hoc Committee contends that the Transmission Providers’ long-term

planning proposal lacks the Ad Hoc Committee’s preferred governance structure – asserting that

an independent evaluator should be used to eliminate potential conflicts of interest when selecting

regional transmission project developers.17 Finally, the Ad Hoc Committee objects to the

Transmission Providers’ proposed tariff revision exempting a Transmission Provider from cost

allocation where they do not have a “reasonable expectation” that they can recover those costs in

retail or wholesale rates.18

        This Answer responds to the Ad Hoc Committee’s October 2 Answer and the contentions

contained therein, explaining why those concerns are misplaced, mischaracterize Order No. 1920,

by the Transmission Providers in the region.

II.    Motion for Leave to Answer

       Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, the

Transmission Providers respectfully move for leave to answer the Ad Hoc Committee’s Answer

in their respective dockets. Rule 213(a)(2) provides that a party may answer a protest in

circumstances where the decisional authority permits the answer for good cause shown. To this

end, the Commission has permitted answers that clarify the record, contribute to an understanding

of the issues, or assist the decision-making process. Because this Answer will clarify the record,

contribute to an understanding of the issues, and assist the Commission in its decision-making

process, good cause exists to grant the Transmission Providers’ motion for leave to file this

Answer.

       The Transmission Providers once again assert that acceptance and consideration of this

Answer is particularly appropriate here due to the significant mandates and changes established

by Order No. 1920 and the discretion afforded to each planning region in developing its Long-

Term Regional Transmission Planning Process in a manner consistent with the directives in Order

No. 1920. This flexibility has resulted in diverse approaches to regional planning and has

generated substantial participation and commentary from a broad range of stakeholders.

III.   Answer

       The Ad Hoc Committee’s proposals do not comply with Order No. 1920 or the FPA.

Furthermore, the Ad Hoc Committee’s proposal is unworkable and will undermine the purpose

of long-term transmission planning, which is to address identified long-term regional needs, not

to make transmission capacity available to the first-moving, highest bidder in an open



                                               -5-
 procurement process – a process designed for entities for which the Transmission Providers have

no obligation to plan, leaving the public utility transmission providers to scramble to solve the

needs of those for whom they have an obligation to plan some other way, at a potentially higher

costs to ratepayers.

         A.       The Ad Hoc Committee’s Answer Does Not Establish that the Commission
                  Should Adopt the Ad Hoc Committee’s Proposals.

         The Ad Hoc Committee’s process for developing both proposals did not produce a

product that commands a convincing degree of support across the WestConnect region. Using

the Commission’s definition,19 the Transmission Providers identified thirteen relevant state

entities (“RSEs”) in the WestConnect region. 20 Several states have multiple RSEs. A state utility

commission therefore is not necessarily the only RSE for a state (and some of the Transmission

Providers are not subject to rate regulation by state commissions). The rationale behind state

engagement was that, given states’ “critical role in transmission planning … facilitating their

engagement” could help minimize delays and costs associated with siting proceedings. 21 Yet

here, fewer than half of the RSEs in the WestConnect region appear as signatories on the Ad Hoc

Committee’s proposal, diminishing the probability of consensus that Order No. 1920 sought to

establish, thereby weakening its persuasiveness.




19
   FERC defined an RSE as “any state entity responsible for electric utility regulation or siting electric transmission
facilities within the state or portion of a state located in the transmission planning region, including any state entity
as may be designated for that purpose by the law of such state.” Building for the Future Through Electric Regional
Transmission Planning and Cost Allocation, Order No. 1920, 187 FERC ¶ 61,068 at P 1355 (2024).
20
   Arizona Corporation Commission; Colorado Public Utilities Commission; Industrial Siting Division of the
Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality; Montana Public Service Commission; Nebraska Public Service
Commission; New Mexico Energy, Minerals, and Natural Resources Department; New Mexico Public Regulation
Commission; New Mexico Renewable Energy Transmission Authority; New Mexico State Land Office; Public
Utility Commission of Texas; South Dakota Public Utilities Commission; Utah Public Service Commission; and
Wyoming Public Service Commission.
21
   Order No. 1920 at P 1362.

                                                          -6-
         The internal voting rules for the CREPC Charter do not resolve the lack of RSE support

regarding the Ad Hoc Committee’s proposals.22 Of thirteen RSEs in the WestConnect planning

region, only six agreed to the proposals. 23 Two of those RSEs are state commissions that did not

agree – Arizona and Texas – whose states represent more than 40% of load in the region.

Additionally, it is still not clear which RSE in states that have multiple RSEs voted in support of

the proposal. While it is true that Order 1920 did not prescribe the threshold required to advance

the proposals,24 that a majority of the possible RSEs did not affirmatively support it is instructive

and goes directly to the weight to be accorded to these proposals. The Transmission Providers do

not contend that the lack of RSE support bars Commission consideration and the Transmission

Providers appreciate the degree to which RSEs and other stakeholders participated in the state

engagement process. Rather, the Transmission Providers note that the RSE proposals are not a

consensus position and should be weighed accordingly.

        B.      The Ad Hoc Committee’s Answer does not cure the defects in the proposed
                ex ante cost allocation methodology.

                1.      Subscription Process Undermines the Ability to Solve Transmission Needs
                        through Long-Term Planning.

        The Ad Hoc Committee has not cured a fatal flaw of their subscription process – the

subscription mechanism permits voluntary funding by anyone (including those for whom the

Transmission Providers have no obligation to plan) in exchange for defined capacity rights in a

long-term regional transmission project that is supposed to serve the long-term needs of those for

whom the Transmission Providers have an obligation to plan. Funding for defined capacity rights

is a central feature of participant funding – which FERC prohibited as a cost allocation


22
   CREPC, Order No. 1920 Ad Hoc Committee Charter (rev. Apr. 22, 2026),
https://www.westernenergyboard.org/wp-content/uploads/1920-ad-hoc-cmte-charter-02132025-_revised4.22.26.pdf.
23
   Ad Hoc Committee Answer at 10.
24
   Order No. 1920 at P 1360.

                                                   -7-
 methodology under the rule.25 While the definition of participant funding is when the “cost of a

transmission facility is allocated only to those entities that volunteer to bear [the cost of a

facility],”26 allocating unsubscribed costs through other mechanisms does not cure the concern

that participant funding disrupts the transmission planning process and leaves other customers

with the remaining capacity regardless of need. 27

        Order No. 1920’s voluntary-funding provisions are different: they allow voluntary

funding to enable a project that “otherwise would not meet the transmission providers’ selection

criteria”28 and they can only be triggered by defined groups with eligibility to do so, not any

interested third party. Despite the Ad Hoc Committee’s efforts to paint their subscription process

as a voluntary funding provision under Order No. 1920, the proposal is a noted departure from

this framework because it allows anyone to subscribe for up to the entire capacity of a project,

including those for whom the Transmission Providers may have absolutely no obligation to plan,

and leaves only the leftover amounts (if any) for those entities the long-term planning process

was designed to serve (without regard to whether this limited capacity would be sufficient to

satisfy the identified long-term regional needs). Whereas the voluntary funding as envisioned

under Order No. 1920 could serve as a lifeline for transmission projects that otherwise would not

get built because they do not meet the criteria for mandatory funding under Order No. 1920, the

subscriber-first process that the Ad Hoc Committee proposes to use for every facility resulting

from long-term regional planning would allow anyone to cut the line and obtain capacity on




25
   See Order No. 1920 at P 1408.
26
   Order No. 1920 at P 1408 n.3008 (citing Order No. 1000, 136 FERC ¶ 61,051 at P 486 n.375) (emphasis added).
27
   Ad Hoc Committee Answer at 15.
28
   Order No. 1920 at P 1013 (emphasis added).

                                                     -8-
 regional projects first – even if those projects are intended to solve the needs of the public utility

transmission providers in the region.

        The Ad Hoc Committee’s proposed solution – allowing Transmission Providers to

subscribe, too – does not resolve the concerns with participant funding. Under that proposal, a

project would first be studied and selected to address identified Transmission Provider needs,

after which its capacity would be subjected to a separate subscription process. A subscription

model necessarily uses price as a tie-breaker to deal with over-subscription the Ad Hoc

Commission proposes no other option,29 resulting in capacity being gobbled up by quick-

moving, deep-pocketed entities, with total disregard of the fact that the tariff process is for the

purpose of serving the long-term needs of the utilities enrolled in the region. This results in the

public utilities needing alternative projects to serve their needs.

        If capacity on a line intended to address a long-term regional need is subscribed, public

utilities enrolled in the region will need to go elsewhere to obtain the capacity required to meet

their long-term transmission needs. For example, if a project is being considered by the region

because it serves various long-term public policy needs, but the project is fully then subscribed

by a large load entity under the subscription process desired by the Ad Hoc Committee (a large

load entity for which no transmission provider enrolled in the region has an obligation to plan),

those long term public policy needs would still need to be addressed by the region. After having

gone through a long-term planning cycle to identify long-term regional needs and after having

evaluated projects to serve those needs, the enrolled Transmission Providers are left with no




29
   The Ad Hoc Committee’s ex-ante cost allocation proposal describes the subscription process as including a 90-
day purchase period and a 60-day negotiation period for the terms and conditions of capacity procurement, subject
to pricing determined by the Project Developer. The proposal discusses a post-subscription process to handle
situations where subscription does not account for all the transmission capacity, but it does not describe what
happens when there is oversubscription. See Ex. D at 7-8.

                                                       -9-
 long-term regional solution, or perhaps an inferior one or multiple inferior projects needed to

serve the same needs. Therefore, a tariff process intended to allow for the selection of a long-

term regional project that is more efficient and cost effective will have failed the core objective

of the tariff, and will have created, instead, inefficiency and ineffectiveness.

          Additionally, questions remain regarding subscriber default that the Ad Hoc Committee

does not address and without which its proposal cannot be considered a workable (let alone

reasonable) alternative. For example, if a subscriber defaults, it is unclear who would be

responsible for covering the defaulting subscriber’s cost of the long-term regional project. Would

those costs be passed on to the Transmission Providers who have been largely squeezed out of

project capacity and driven to solve their transmission needs through other projects? In addition,

how does this work on right-sized facilities? As proposed by the Ad Hoc Committee, a

subscriber would be allowed take 100% of the capacity of a right-sized facility that is part of an

existing transmission network, potentially severing existing transmission paths.

                  2.      DFAX Methodology Depends on “Zones” That Do Not Exist.

          The Ad Hoc Committee’s Answer does not resolve the WestConnect-specific

implementation problem: WestConnect has no established transmission zones and includes

overlapping transmission systems and non-jurisdictional utilities. The Ad Hoc Committee asserts

that the Commission has already found that DFAX is just and reasonable in PJM, that DFAX

could be well suited to identify the way higher voltage levels produce benefits over a wider

area.30 Unlike in regions where zones generally correspond to distinct utility footprints or

operational boundaries, the WestConnect footprint features substantial overlap among

transmission assets and utility service territories. As a result, there are no coherent or stable


30
     Ad Hoc Committee Answer at 18-19.

                                                - 10 -
 zones that can be consistently defined for purposes of cost allocation. DFAX is a reasonable

methodology to apply in PJM with its clearly defined zones. However, in the WestConnect

region, a DFAX-based allocation approach is impracticable because the identifiable zones to

map power flows and allocate costs that DFAX methodologies rely upon do not exist.

                   3.       De Minimis Threshold Creates Free Riders.

           The proposed 2% de minimis threshold would excuse identified beneficiaries from cost

responsibility. As noted in the Transmission Providers’ August 5 Answer, if multiple

beneficiaries are below the 2% threshold, a significant cost could be shifted onto other

beneficiaries. Ultimately, this will result in Transmission Providers’ ratepayers cross-subsidizing

other energy customers. At a time when rising energy costs are a major concern, such cross-

subsidization should be avoided.

           The costs of regional facilities must be assigned in a manner that is “roughly

commensurate” to the benefits those projects provide. 31 To be sure, this standard permits

reasonable approximation. However, it does not itself justify a categorical exemption that

reallocates costs attributable to identified beneficiaries – entities that receive quantified benefits

studied and identified at the direction of the Commission. In Consolidated Edison, the

Commission found PJM’s de minimis exemption it had previously approved was unduly

discriminatory because its application produced distorted cost allocations among transmission

zones of different sizes, exempting larger zones from cost responsibility despite their significant

use of transmission facilities while shifting disproportionate costs to smaller zones. 32 The Ad



31
  Ill. Commerce Comm’n v. FERC, 756 F.3d 556, 559 (7th Cir. 2014) (explaining that FERC must have “an
articulable and plausible reason to believe that the benefits are at least roughly commensurate with those utilities’
share of total electricity sales in PJM’s region” (quoting Ill. Commerce Comm’n v. FERC, 576 F.3d 470, 477 (7th
Cir. 2009))).
32
     Consol. Edison Co. of New York, Inc., 194 FERC ¶ 61,179 (2026).

                                                        - 11 -
 Hoc Committee, trying to use this case to illustrate that FERC has approved a de minimis

exception in the past, acknowledges FERC’s holding that its application was discriminatory. 33

However, the Ad Hoc Committee ignores FERC’s reasoning – the Commission found the de

minimis exception’s application was discriminatory because of how it distorted the way costs

were allocated across zones.34 While WestConnect does not have zones, cost allocation could be

distorted across the entire WestConnect footprint if multiple customers are below the 2%

threshold.

           The de minimis exception proffered by the Ad Hoc Committee is also directly contrary to

binding precedent on regional cost allocation in the WestConnect region. In El Paso Electric Co.

v. FERC, the Fifth Circuit held that the cost allocation principle does not authorize FERC to

force jurisdictional utilities to assume the costs of providing service to non-jurisdictional utilities,

and emphasized that FERC may not sacrifice cost causation by refusing to allocate costs to those

who cause costs to be incurred and reap resulting benefits. 35 The Ad Hoc Committee tries to

argue that El Paso does not apply to these circumstances because all the entities involved are

FERC jurisdictional utilities.36 But that ignores the fundamental holding of the case – that

utilities should not be forced to cross-subsidize the costs necessary to provide benefits to other

entities. In the El Paso case, the jurisdictional status was the underlying issue that created this

free ridership problem, but the legal error was the free ridership. Under the Ad Hoc Committee’s

proposal, it is asking FERC to mandate free ridership – utilities having their long-term

transmission needs planned for and solved through Order No. 1920’s long-term transmission



33
     Ad Hoc Committee Answer at 20.
34
     Consol. Edison Co. of New York, Inc., 194 FERC ¶ 61,179, at PP 35, 56 (2026).
35
     El Paso Elec. Co. v. FERC, 76 F.4th 352, 363 (5th Cir. 2023).
36
     Ad Hoc Committee Answer at 20-21.

                                                         - 12 -
 planning while also avoiding cost responsibility because their share falls below the arbitrary line

drawn by some portion of the Ad Hoc Committee’s representatives that endorses the proposal.

         C.        The Ad Hoc Committee’s Answer Does Not Resolve the Concerns with the
                   State Agreement Process Itself.

         The core issue in evaluating the proposed State Agreement Process for determining

alternative cost allocations following project selection is whether the resulting proposed

provisions are consistent with Order No. 1920 and the FPA and a just and reasonable approach to

long-term regional transmission cost allocation. Two major issues remain unresolved with the

proposed decision-making process that the selected state commissions would employ under the

State Agreement Process proposed by the Ad Hoc Committee.

         First, the Ad Hoc Committee’s proposal raises serious representation concerns. The Ad

Hoc Committee’s proposed State Agreement Process limits voting to state commissions that

regulate retail rates – omitting key state entities responsible for siting electric transmission

facilities.37 Excluding entities responsible for siting transmission projects from the State

Agreement Process creates a significant risk that the cost allocations developed and made public

through the long-term planning process and shared with stakeholders, including the full range of

RSEs, could be changed by a subset of RSEs and result in a loss of key regulatory support for

siting the actual facilities. This approach also deprives certain WestConnect Transmission

Providers that are not subject to state retail-rate regulation of a voting representative to protect

their interests and those of their customers. Without such representation, there is a risk of an

over-allocation of costs to the Transmission Provider(s) without a voting representative.




37
   See Order No. 1920 at P 44 “Relevant State Entity is any state entity responsible for electric utility regulation or
siting electric transmission facilities within the state or portion of a state located in the transmission planning region,
including any state entity as may be designated for that purpose by the law of such state.”

                                                          - 13 -
            Second, although the Transmission Providers do not oppose providing relevant

information to RSEs to help them evaluate potential projects, the Ad Hoc Committee’s Answer

does not justify granting a state the entitlement to direct information requests to Transmission

Providers outside their jurisdiction. As the Transmission Providers have noted, WestConnect is

not a legal entity to which such information requests can be directed to and handled. 38

Additionally, it is unreasonable to expect the Transmission Providers to have to deal with a

scattershot of information requests from regulators with whom they do not have a working

relationship and who do not regulate them. It is more organized and efficient to rely on existing

regulatory relationships by structuring the information-request process to provide relevant

information to an RSE through the specific Transmission Provider(s) subject to the RSE’s

jurisdiction.

           D.        The Ad Hoc Committee’s other arguments do not demonstrate
                     noncompliance.

                     1.          Order No. 1920 Does Not Require an Independent Evaluator, Which
                                 Would Create Unnecessary Planning Risks.

           The Ad Hoc Committee acknowledges that Order No. 1920 does not require an

independent evaluator.39 Indeed, multiple regions have no such independent evaluator for Order

1000 transmission planning, and indeed, the non-RTO regions that have submitted Order No.

1920 compliance filings have proposed no such entity. As such, just and reasonable transmission

planning cannot be reasonably found to require such an entity. Indeed, imposing one over the

wishes of the public utilities in the region would contravene the same kind of FPA prohibition

that the courts identified in finding that the Commission does not have the power to require



38
     Transmittal Letter at 48.
39
     Ad Hoc Committee Answer at P 26.

                                                      - 14 -
 public utilities to join an RTO.40 The Ad Hoc Committee’s preference for one therefore does not

establish that the Transmission Providers’ proposal is noncompliant. The Commission should

approve the Transmission Providers’ proposal without this unnecessary and unlawful feature.

           An independent evaluator would also strip the public utilities of their existing authority

over transmission planning, creating significant risk. The public utilities have an obligation to

plan their transmission systems to address the needs of their transmission customers. This

“independent evaluator” has no such obligation. As a result, using an independent evaluator

would create a disconnect between the entity with authority over long-term transmission

planning and the public utilities, which have the responsibility, under both state and federal law,

to ensure appropriate transmission planning and adequacy of service.

                    2.          The Cost-Recovery Language Remains Appropriate.

           The Ad Hoc Committee challenges the Transmission Providers’ inclusion of a provision

from their Order No. 1000 tariffs, which the Commission previously approved, that relieves the

Transmission Providers from cost responsibility for Long-Term Transmission Facilities from

which they do not expect to be able to reasonably recover in their rates. 41 In accepting the

Transmission Providers’ Order No. 1000 provisions, the Commission made a specific reference

to this provision in its compliance order, without any changes mandated. 42 The Ad Hoc

Committee’s Answer identifies no Order No. 1920 requirement compelling its removal. 43 They



40

FERC does not have the power to compel participation in RTOs); Pub. Util. Dist. No. 1 of Snohomish Cnty. v.
FERC, 272 F.3d 607, 614 (D.C. Cir. 2001) (“Order 2000, by its own terms, does not mandate RTO participation.”).
41
     Attach. E, Section IX.J.
42

owners will not assume cost responsibility for a transmission project if the cost of the project is not reasonably
expected to be recoverable in its retail or wholesale transmission rates.”).
43
     Ad Hoc Committee Answer at 27.

                                                         - 15 -
 argue that exempting the Transmission Providers from these costs could lead to cross-

subsidization, but ignore that requiring utilities to bear costs that cannot be recovered in rates

would not be just and reasonable and would also be confiscatory under the Fifth Amendment. 44

IV.      Conclusion

         For these reasons, the Transmission Providers request that the Commission accept this

answer, deny the protests and comments filed by certain intervenors as discussed above, and accept

the June 12th Compliance Filings of the Transmission Providers.
